nodes.label: Pravasi Sangama 2026 E-Ticketing & Gate Management
nodes.rationale: Enterprise e-ticketing and gate-control platform for the Karnataka Cultural Foundation's Pravasi Sangama 2026 event. Agents in the field issue tickets, gate staff scan QR codes, a superuser watches live. Stack: Next.js App Router + TypeScript + Tailwind frontend, Express + Postgres (raw pg, SQL migrations, no heavy ORM) backend, JWT two-tier auth, socket.io realtime.

nodes.label: Five-Role Nested Hierarchy
nodes.rationale: Superuser -> Division -> Unit -> (Unit Admin, Agent). The hierarchy is strictly nested so every ticket traces back to exactly one agent, in one unit, in one division. Strict nesting is what makes bottom-up authorization expressible as a single SQL predicate rather than an application-level check.

nodes.label: Superuser
nodes.rationale: Full system access: real-time analytics, audit logs, ticket revocation, division/unit/agent CRUD, kill switches. Single account tier with no delegated admin, deliberately — delegation is done by the separate Unit Admin table rather than by grading superuser accounts.

nodes.label: Division (District)
nodes.rationale: A geographical grouping owning many units. Read access to its own subtree's analytics and ticket ledger only; cannot see other divisions.

nodes.label: Sector
nodes.rationale: Parent grouping of units held as units.sector (migration 010), twelve values (BATHA, BADIYA, SHIFA, MALAZ, MUROOJ, GHURNATHA, OLAYA, RABVA, SUDAIR, MUZAMIYYAH, SANAYIYYAH, KHARJ). Deliberately a normalised text column, NOT a sectors table: a sector is a name and nothing else today, so a table would buy referential integrity at the price of a join on every ledger and analytics query. Migration 010's header records what would have to change to promote it if a sector ever grows attributes.

nodes.label: Unit
nodes.rationale: A specific physical location within a division. The unit is the scope every agent token carries and every ticket is written against. It is NOT an authentication factor for an agent's own login — unit is derived server-side from the agent's row — but a unit-scoped invite PIN gates the agent portal before the login form is reachable.

nodes.label: Unit Admin
nodes.rationale: Migration 005. Decentralises agent approval: a named person's account scoped to one unit whose only capability is approving/rejecting agent registrations for that unit — no analytics, no ledger, no CRUD. Exists to remove the superuser as the sole approval bottleneck across 30+ locations run by non-technical volunteers. Deliberately a unit_admins table, not a repurposed agents row, and unrelated to the deleted unit-login flow despite both saying 'unit': that authenticated a location, this is a named person's account.

nodes.label: Agent
nodes.rationale: The human issuing tickets, assigned to one unit, identified by mobile number ONLY — agents.email stopped being unique in migration 013 so agents without a personal address can share their unit head's. Cannot access analytics, cannot edit or revoke issued tickets, and can only see registrations from their own unit.

nodes.label: Bottom-Up Authorization Rule
nodes.rationale: Authorization is always evaluated bottom-up from the token's unitId -> divisionId. Never trust a client-supplied division or unit id on a write path. Enforced as a SQL predicate keyed on the caller's own unit_admins.id rather than an application-level check a reviewer could miss — a row outside scope matches zero rows at the database level, not 'filtered out after the fact'.

nodes.label: decideAgent restrictToAdminId Predicate
nodes.rationale: admin.repository.decideAgent takes an optional restrictToAdminId; when set it resolves the full union of the caller's direct unit_id and supervisor_unit_assignments in one SQL predicate. Superuser calls pass no restrictToAdminId, which is what 'ultimate authority' means concretely. Known gap: it only matches approval_status = 'PENDING', so an auto-approved agent can never be rejected.

nodes.label: supervisor_unit_assignments (Zone Supervisor Coverage)
nodes.rationale: Migration 007 many-to-many mapping table (admin_id, unit_id). Chosen as Option B over widening unit_admins.unit_id. Zone Supervisors (ZON01-ZON03) have NULL unit_id and one row per covered unit; the two mechanisms compose. Seeded with a deliberately non-geographic placeholder 10/10/10 chunk in array declaration order so every zone dashboard is populated and testable out of the box — must be replaced with the real split before the event. Insert is ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING so reruns only add; removal is manual by design, same as a wrongly-approved agent isn't auto-corrected.

nodes.label: Unit Gateway
nodes.rationale: Migration 009. POST /api/auth/unit-gateway checks a unit code + 4-digit agent_invite_pin against units.agent_invite_pin_hash and returns the unit's public info — no cookie, no JWT, no unit_sessions row. Deliberately narrower than the deleted two-step unit-login it echoes: ONE PIN PER UNIT, not per agent, which is what defuses the original manpower objection. It is a UX gate against misassignment, NOT a security boundary — hence 4 digits rather than the unit admin's password. The real boundary is server-side re-verification inside agentSignup. Removed once as non-negotiable, then reinstated on an explicit informed decision by the project owner; do not 'fix' it away again without asking.

nodes.label: Sticky Unit Gateway
nodes.rationale: Third iteration: the gate is now asked ONCE PER DEVICE rather than before every sign-in — the frequency, not the gate, was the real complaint. frontend/src/lib/unitGateway.ts writes unit_code, unit name and cleared-at to localStorage; the PIN is NEVER stored, because these are shared phones and devtools would leak it. That omission is what keeps the gate meaningful: signing in on a sticky device needs no PIN (zero friction, the common case) but REGISTERING re-asks, so a borrowed phone cannot mint a new ticket issuer. ActiveUnit.invitePin is string|null, held in React state only. A successful sign-in re-saves the unit from the server's answer so a wrongly-set device self-corrects. A 'Change' control clears it for devices moving between units.

nodes.label: Agent Login (single-step)
nodes.rationale: POST /api/auth/agent-login is mobile number + password, nothing else. unitId/divisionId are read from agents.unit_id joined to units.division_id AFTER the password verifies, so the client never names a unit and an agent structurally cannot issue against a unit they are not assigned to — the old 'does the agent match the step-1 unit?' comparison became structural. Password is verified before anything else is disclosed: approval state (PENDING/REJECTED) is revealed only after a correct password so the endpoint cannot enumerate registered numbers. JWT carries {agentId, unitId, divisionId, sessionId, role:'AGENT'}.

nodes.label: Deleted UNIT_PENDING / unit-login Flow
nodes.rationale: POST /api/auth/unit-login, the UNIT_PENDING role and every partially-authenticated branch were deleted from packages/shared (AUTH_ROLES, UnitPendingClaims, UnitLoginSchema), backend (route, controller, service, findUnitsByCode, createUnitSession, findLiveSession, bindAgentToSession, agentNotBound) and frontend (middleware.ts, ProtectedRoute, useAuthStore.setUnitPending). units.access_code_hash is still on the table and seeded but NOTHING READS IT — the Unit Gateway deliberately did not revive it, because that column was NOT NULL and wired into the unit_sessions/UNIT_PENDING machinery; reusing it would drag those assumptions back. Giving it a reader would be a third distinct decision.

nodes.label: What the Single-Step Login Gave Up
nodes.rationale: Stated honestly rather than papered over: a stolen agent password is now sufficient alone from any device anywhere, where it previously also needed physical presence at an unlocked unit; and unit_sessions no longer records a location opened independently of the people who used it, so the audit trail is per-agent not per-post. Compensating controls that now matter more: agent approval, fast deactivation via is_active, AGENT_LOGIN/AGENT_LOGIN_FAILED audit rows, and the login rate limiter.

nodes.label: JWTs in httpOnly Cookies
nodes.rationale: JWTs live in httpOnly cookies, never localStorage — these are shared phones. The sticky gateway's localStorage use does not weaken this because no token, session or credential is written there; it is a device preference and the cookie remains the only thing that authenticates.

nodes.label: Shared Email, Mobile-Only Identity (migration 013)
nodes.rationale: agents.email lost UNIQUE because many field agents have no address of their own and register under their unit head's. Email is therefore a contact field, not an identifier; mobile_number stays UNIQUE and IS the Agent ID. Two things depended on the dropped uniqueness and both had to change: login became mobile-only (a shared address makes LIMIT 1 return an arbitrary agent), and self-service reset became mobile-keyed.

nodes.label: Self-Service Password Reset (mobile-keyed)
nodes.rationale: POST /api/auth/forgot-password -> POST /api/auth/reset-password, landing on /login/reset?token=. Keyed on MOBILE NUMBER never email: looking an agent up by a shared address returns an arbitrary one of them, so the link could be minted for a DIFFERENT agent than the one who asked. What it does NOT fix: several agents genuinely sharing an inbox can all open the link — keying on mobile fixes who the token is minted for, not who reaches the mailbox. Bounded by 30-minute expiry, single use (consumed_at IS NULL), one live token per agent, AGENT_PASSWORD_RESET_REQUESTED audit row. Always answers 202 with the same body whether or not the number exists, so it cannot enumerate the roster — same reasoning that hides approval state behind a correct password. Carries signupLimiter (10/hour/IP) not loginLimiter, because it mails a third party on an unauthenticated request. No session is issued on success, so a stolen link cannot also hand over a live session.

nodes.label: Rotate-and-Reveal Password Recovery
nodes.rationale: Admin-driven recovery rotates the password and reveals it once (POST /api/unit-admin/agents/:id/reset-password, POST /api/admin/agents/:id/reset-password), audited as AGENT_PASSWORD_RESET. Deliberately UNLIKE the readable unit invite PIN, and the inconsistency is intentional: the PIN is 4 digits, already committed to the repo, and explicitly not an access control, whereas an agent password authorises ISSUING TICKETS and agents choose their own — people reuse passwords, so storing them readably would expose credentials those volunteers use on other services, which is harm beyond this event. The operational need is 'my agent can't sign in', and a fresh password meets it completely. Signup password is optional; a blank one generates psa<4 digits>-pw shown once, so an account is never created without a credential.

nodes.label: Simplified Onboarding (Unit Admin tier OFF)
nodes.rationale: The multi-step flow proved too complex for field staff, so the architecture was flattened: registrations auto-approve (createSelfRegisteredAgent inserts APPROVED), and Unit Admin is hidden from /management. NOTHING WAS DELETED — the login endpoint, unit_admins rows and /unit/dashboard are untouched, so turning the tier back on is re-exposing it, not rebuilding it. Consequence flagged loudly: the invite PIN is now the ONLY barrier to minting a ticket issuer, since approval and PIN used to be two independent checks and auto-approval removed one.

nodes.label: Invite PIN as Sole Barrier to Minting an Issuer
nodes.rationale: Drop the PIN and anyone who finds /login can self-register and issue real tickets. This was raised explicitly and keeping the PIN on signup was the decision. Two open gaps make it worse: ticket revocation is unbuilt (a fraudulent ticket needs direct SQL), and decideAgent only matches PENDING so an auto-approved agent can never be rejected — which is why POST /api/admin/agents/:id/active exists as the only in-app way to switch off an account auto-approval let in.

nodes.label: /unit/dashboard (Unit Admin Screen)
nodes.rationale: Deliberately NOT AdminShell: no nav rail, no analytics, no CRUD — one screen, one job, for a volunteer who may never have used the rest of the system. Pending agents get two buttons sized to be unmissable on a phone in daylight. An admin with neither unit_id nor assignments renders an explicit 'No unit assigned yet' screen rather than guessing a scope or showing everything. Below is a read-only Ticket Sales table (GET /api/unit-admin/tickets) scoped by unitAdminTicketWhere() — visibility, not navigation.

nodes.label: unitAdminTicketWhere() Scope Predicate
nodes.rationale: The ONLY predicate deciding which ticket rows exist for a unit-admin caller, baked into the query rather than filtered after the fact, mirroring decideAgent's restrictToAdminId. Row shape (AdminTicketRow) is shared with the superuser ledger — a ticket's data doesn't change depending on who's allowed to see it, only which rows come back.

nodes.label: db:provision-units (provision-unit-admins.ts)
nodes.rationale: Creates the 30 real units, 33 unit_admins rows (30 location + 3 Zone Supervisors), the zone assignment rows, and each unit's agent_invite_pin_hash. Deliberately NOT db:seed: this is real event data meant to run once against production, so it has no NODE_ENV guard — but it is idempotent and safe to re-run. Invite PINs are printed in the report unlike the admin passwords, because a unit head has to keep reciting the PIN to agents rather than using it once themselves. The 33 passwords are short, guessable (<code>PW) and committed in plaintext, mirroring the gate-PIN trade; rotate every one before the event.

nodes.label: db:bulk-rotate-passwords
nodes.rationale: Generates <sector><4 digits>-pw (BAD01 -> bad0846-pw): all lowercase so no shift key, the only variable part a digit run a numeric keypad handles, because staff are coming off paper systems and type on phones. Prints once to console as the distribution list, never to a file. Carries only 4 digits of entropy (10,000/account) since the prefix derives from the public username and -pw is constant — ~20x weaker than the Bat01-7kX format it replaced, chosen deliberately on instruction with the tradeoff stated. What stands behind it: loginLimiter (20/15min/IP, ~125h to exhaust one account from one IP; a multi-IP spray is the real exposure), role-bounded blast radius (a unit admin cannot issue, revoke, scan or reach another unit — worst case is a rogue agent being approved), and AGENT_APPROVED/AGENT_REJECTED audit rows carrying the approving admin id. If unacceptable, raise DIGIT_COUNT rather than reintroducing letters — each digit is 10x the space for one keypress.

nodes.label: QR Fan-Out and Capacity
nodes.rationale: Normal = 1 person, 1 QR (GUEST). VIP/VVIP/SVIP = 4 persons, 5 QR (4 GUEST + 1 LOCATION). The three premium tiers are IDENTICAL in capacity and differ only in presentation, pricing and access zone — never in seat count.

nodes.label: Printed Panels Differ From Database Rows
nodes.rationale: The pass prints 2 panels for Normal (1 Location + 1 Guest) and 5 for premium (1 Location + 4 Guest). Every Location panel on every tier encodes VENUE_INFO_URL — the fixed Google Maps link — not the backend's LOCATION payload, because that payload is a bare UUID: a guest pointing a camera at it gets nothing, where the URL opens directions. Normal has no LOCATION row at all, so its panel is added by the component; qrCodePlanFor() is untouched — this is print layout, not fan-out. Deliberately accepted consequence: premium LOCATION rows still exist in qr_codes but are never printed, so the gate's LOCATION_INFO path is unreachable from a scanned pass. Those rows are inert.

nodes.label: Children Below 12
nodes.rationale: Free and EXCLUDED from ticket capacity: they consume no guest QR and do not increment countedPersons. Recorded on the registration for catering and crowd-safety headcount only. Surfaced read-only in three places (ticket stub, pass footer, agent ledger column) and printed even when zero — a gate reading '+0 Children' knows the field was captured, where a missing line is ambiguous.

nodes.label: Backend Is the Authority on Capacity
nodes.rationale: The frontend is a convenience. countedPersons is derived, never user-editable, and re-derived server-side on write — a client posting {ticketType:'Normal', countedPersons:4} must be rejected, not trusted. QR fan-out happens server-side at issuance, each row independently scannable and consumable. Gate scans are idempotent. The Location QR is never an admission credential and must never decrement guest capacity.

nodes.label: Sequential Request and Ticket Numbering (migration 016)
nodes.rationale: REQ-0001 / TKT-0001, 4 digits, no letters, one global counter each shared across every unit. This REVERSES the original crypto-random design on explicit instruction: sequential numbers leak total sales volume (the holder of TKT-0350 knows 350 were sold) and make the range enumerable rather than sparse. That cost is real and was accepted knowingly, because NEITHER NUMBER IS AN ADMISSION CREDENTIAL — the exposure is commercial, not a gate breach. Four digits is sized to the event (9,999 is ~20x expected attendance), not to collision math, since sequential allocation has no collisions to absorb. Leading zeros are significant. Older-format tickets keep their numbers and stay searchable.

nodes.label: Postgres Sequence Allocation (nextTicketNumbers)
nodes.rationale: request_number_seq / ticket_number_seq are drawn via tickets.repository.nextTicketNumbers() inside the issuing transaction. nextval never hands the same value to two callers so concurrent agents cannot collide; SELECT MAX(...)+1 would race exactly the way a read-then-write races at the gate. There is deliberately NO generator in lib/identifiers.ts any more — that would be a second source of truth for a value only the sequence can make unique. Sequences do not roll back, so a failed issuance leaves a gap: correct, because a gap is invisible except to someone reconciling counts whereas a reused number means two tickets share an identifier. Do not count tickets by reading the last number.

nodes.label: Format With to_char, Never LPAD
nodes.rationale: Postgres LPAD TRUNCATES when the value exceeds the width — LPAD('687223',4,'0') is '6872' silently. Not cosmetic: truncation is not injective, so two sequence values can collapse to one printed number and destroy the uniqueness the sequence exists to provide. It also makes sequential numbers look random since the visible digits are the tail of a larger counter. This shipped once and was caught in testing. to_char(n,'FM0000') pads to width and GROWS past it instead of cutting.

nodes.label: QR Payload Secrecy (SHA-256, never stored)
nodes.rationale: Issuance generates a UUID per code, stores sha256(payload) in qr_codes.qr_hash, and returns raw payloads ONCE in the issuance response. They are unrecoverable afterwards, so reissuing a lost ticket means new codes and revoking the old ones. SHA-256 rather than bcrypt is deliberate: the payload is a 122-bit random value, not a password — there is no dictionary to attack, and the gate needs one indexed lookup rather than a per-row comparison.

nodes.label: packages/shared as Single Source of Truth
nodes.rationale: SEATS_PER_TIER, PREMIUM_TICKET_TYPES, qrCodeCountFor() and qrCodePlanFor() live in packages/shared/src/constants.ts and are imported by both tiers. Nothing in frontend/ or backend/ may re-declare them: if the issuer and the scanner ever disagree about what 'VIP' means, the gate admits the wrong number of people — the highest-severity class of bug in the system. Canonical tier values are UPPERCASE matching the Postgres enum; TICKET_TYPE_LABELS is display-only and must never be persisted or transmitted. Consumed as COMPILED output, so any src edit is invisible until npm run build:shared.

nodes.label: Apple-like Minimalist Design Language
nodes.rationale: Extreme restraint: generous whitespace, few borders, no gradients on UI surfaces; if a divider can be omitted, omit it. Cards pure white rounded-3xl with a soft diffuse shadow and hairline ring, never a hard drop shadow. Glassmorphism reserved for FLOATING elements only, never static content cards. Radii are continuous (xl inputs -> 2xl buttons -> 3xl page cards -> full pills), never mixed arbitrarily. Brand carried as accent, not chrome.

nodes.label: Motion Vocabulary (springs, reducedMotion)
nodes.rationale: Anything entering or leaving the tree uses framer-motion springs from lib/motion.ts, never an ad-hoc tween; damping never drops below ~26 so surfaces settle rather than overshoot. CSS transitions stay for hover and press; springs are for presence. MotionConfig reducedMotion='user' wraps the app because the scanner throws full-screen colour several times a minute and a motion-sensitive agent works a six-hour shift.

nodes.label: Toasts vs Inline State
nodes.rationale: Toasts carry transient OUTCOMES (wrong PIN, email sent, PDF saved). Persistent STATE (offline, pending sync, reconnecting) stays inline where it can be read at any moment. Never put a gate's connection status in something that disappears.

nodes.label: Official Brand Palette
nodes.rationale: Violet #5E17EB is the single action colour everywhere (7.5:1 on white); Violet Deep #37098C and Violet Dark #2E0775 are dark surfaces; Amber #FFA51F and Amber Light #FFD79A are accents ON DARK VIOLET ONLY. #5E17EB and #37098C are not interchangeable and one value cannot replace both: the action colour must read on white, the ticket surface must let amber read on it — amber on #5E17EB is 3.81:1 (fine for display type, failing at the 8-10px the ticket sets eyebrows in) versus 6.74:1 on #37098C. Amber on white is 1.97:1 and unreadable, the same trap the previous gold had at 2.10:1. Mastheads are white because the logo artwork is dark violet and ~59% of its ink measures 1.0-1.5:1 on the old navy. There is NO navy or gold in this system — #062B59 and #D4AF37 are regressions if they reappear, and #800000 maroon was retired earlier.

nodes.label: Semantic Colours (exempt and universal)
nodes.rationale: Emerald = admitted/success, amber-600 = duplicate/pending, red = invalid/error. Never re-themed to brand colours because a gate agent reads them pre-linguistically. The semantic amber is Tailwind's, not brand-amber — different values doing different jobs.

nodes.label: chartTheme.ts Chart Palette
nodes.rationale: A separate, validated set deliberately independent of the brand, audited for categorical distinction on white; do not substitute brand violet into it beyond BAR_VIOLET, the single-series bar with no adjacent hue to separate from. CLIENT_STAGE_COLORS is a separate palette from TIER_COLORS because sharing a ramp would paint 'VIP' and 'Confirmed' the same colour on one dashboard. The first attempt reused STATUS_TONE's emerald/red and FAILED CVD validation at deltaE 5.6 (deutan) — a deuteranope could not separate CONFIRMED from DECLINED, the most consequential distinction on screen; re-stepped to deltaE 11.0. PROSPECT is deliberately near-gray and fails the chroma floor on purpose: it is the 'not started' baseline and a saturated hue would give the largest, least interesting bucket the most visual weight.

nodes.label: Montserrat via next/font
nodes.rationale: Loaded via next/font/google in app/layout.tsx, NOT a CSS @import: next/font self-hosts the files so the gate PWA still renders correctly offline, whereas a Google Fonts import is a runtime request to a third-party origin the service worker is forbidden from caching. Apple's type scale does not align with Tailwind's defaults, so explicit pixel sizes are used; tight tracking on large text and wide tracking on small uppercase text is most of the 'Apple' feel.

nodes.label: Two-Layer Focus Ring
nodes.rationale: The signature interaction detail: every focusable input uses BOTH a border tightening and a wide soft ring (focus:border-[#5E17EB]/40 focus:ring-4 focus:ring-[#5E17EB]/10), approximating the macOS focus glow which a single ring cannot. Error state swaps the hue, never the structure.

nodes.label: Derived State via useMemo
nodes.rationale: Anything computable from other state is computed with useMemo, never mirrored into its own useState — duplicated state drifts, and in this system drift means wrong admission counts. Read-only derived inputs get readOnly AND tabIndex={-1} so keyboard users don't land on a dead field.

nodes.label: Print/PDF Pipeline (window.print, not rasteriser)
nodes.rationale: lib/printTicket.ts sets data-printing='ticket' on <html>, globals.css's @media print hides everything except [data-print-ticket], and the browser lays out the page itself so text and QR stay VECTOR. The old html2canvas+jsPDF path produced a PDF of pixels and, because html2canvas approximates line boxes rather than implementing CSS layout, clipped descenders and mis-centred badges no matter how padding was tuned — do not reintroduce it. Never set line-height:normal on the pass: html2canvas resolves 'normal' with its own approximation, so every text node carries an explicit px line-height. html2canvas correctly remains for the PNG shared over WhatsApp, where the output is an image anyway.

nodes.label: Overlays Are display:none While Printing
nodes.rationale: visibility:hidden keeps the element tree intact, and hidden elements still occupy layout — a viewport-covering position:fixed overlay with a backdrop-filter leaks into the PDF anyway, which is how the share modal ended up printed on top of the ticket. globals.css therefore display:none's [role=dialog], the sonner toaster and anything marked data-print-hide; a new overlay only needs that attribute. Never widen those selectors to something that could wrap the ticket. ShareTicketModal also unmounts and waits two frames before window.print() — an element not in the document cannot be laid out at all, whatever the browser does; the CSS is the backstop. globals.css must carry print-color-adjust:exact or browsers strip the violet ticket fill and print a white rectangle.

nodes.label: Defensive UI Fallbacks
nodes.rationale: Optional data drives STATE, not blank space: no email on file renders a disabled 'No Email Available' pill, not a hidden button. Branch layouts fill their own gaps — a Normal ticket renders an 'Admits 1 Person' block instead of four empty QR slots. Props carry sensible defaults so every component renders standalone for review without a live backend. Client validation is a courtesy, never a control.

nodes.label: Feature-Sliced Backend
nodes.rationale: Backend is feature-sliced (modules/tickets/*), not layer-sliced, so a ticket change touches one folder. 'use client' only where interactivity genuinely requires it. Local UI primitives live at the bottom of their consuming file until a SECOND screen needs them, then graduate to components/ui/ — don't pre-abstract. Placeholder implementations carry a comment naming their real replacement.

nodes.label: Offline-First Gate Scanning Architecture
nodes.rationale: Event day is the only day that matters: hundreds of scans per minute, venue wifi under load, agents on shared phones. The governing principle is that A SCAN IS A CLAIM, NOT A FACT — the client records claims, the server resolves them into admissions, and nothing at the gate blocks on a round trip. Non-negotiables: the gate never blocks on the network; every scan attempt is recorded; the conditional UPDATE is the only admission mechanism; PENDING SYNC is visually distinct from confirmed admission; client_scan_id makes every sync retry idempotent; location codes never admit and never consume capacity.

nodes.label: POST /api/scan/verify
nodes.rationale: Single point lookup on the UNIQUE qr_codes.qr_hash index, one transaction, no joins on the hot path; target p99 < 50ms server-side with the whole gate interaction budgeted at 300ms. ALWAYS HTTP 200 with a status discriminant — a duplicate is not a client error but a valid expected answer the gate UI must render loudly. This matters most offline: the queue treats any non-2xx as 'network problem, retry later', so returning 409 for a duplicate would make scanners retry a settled verdict forever. Two deliberate levels: status (SUCCESS|DUPLICATE|INVALID, the only field the UI branches on) and reason (the precise cause, mapped to scan_logs.result via SCAN_REASON_TO_RESULT in shared). Also carries codeKind, guestIndex and replay:true.

nodes.label: Conditional UPDATE (the row is the lock)
nodes.rationale: Two scanners hitting the same QR in the same millisecond is not hypothetical at a four-guest VIP ticket. DO NOT READ-THEN-WRITE: the UPDATE guards on status='ISSUED' AND code_kind='GUEST' AND joined tickets.status='ACTIVE', so exactly one transaction matches. Zero rows means the caller diagnoses why with a follow-up read. No SELECT FOR UPDATE, no advisory locks, no application mutex — the row is the lock. Revocation is enforced in the SAME statement by joining tickets, because a separate pre-check would race. Location codes are never consumed: guests rescan the venue pass all evening and burning it on first use would turn every later scan into a false duplicate.

nodes.label: Scanner PWA with IndexedDB Queue
nodes.rationale: Stores scan_queue, known_codes and local_admits in IndexedDB (idb-keyval). Online: POST /verify with a 1500ms timeout, but the scan is written to scan_queue BEFORE the request and marked SYNCED on success — created before, not after, or a response lost in flight loses the scan. Offline fallback is triggered by timeout, network error or 5xx, NOT by navigator.onLine which lies on captive venue wifi. The UI shows an unmistakable amber PENDING SYNC because staff must tell admitted-and-confirmed from admitted-and-unverified at a glance. The gate ADMITS on a pending scan: holding a queue at the door to wait for wifi is worse than the failure mode it prevents.

nodes.label: Service Worker Scope (shell only)
nodes.rationale: public/sw.js caches the SHELL ONLY; every /api/* request passes through untouched with no respondWith at all. Scan durability is the app's job (IndexedDB queue + bulk-sync); a worker that cached or replayed an admission would corrupt exactly the headcount the queue exists to protect. Navigations are network-first with a 3s timeout, not stale-while-revalidate — serving stale HTML that references purged build chunks produces a white screen at a gate.

nodes.label: POST /api/scan/bulk-sync
nodes.rationale: A worker drains the queue when the network returns, via Background Sync API where available and a 5s interval with exponential backoff elsewhere. Batch <= 200 per request, oldest first. client_scan_id (client-generated UUID) is the idempotency key so replays after a half-delivered batch are free: the insert is ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING and the stored result is returned. The client's scanned_at wins for ordering so offline scans replay in the order they physically happened, not arrival order; clock skew is bounded by stamping a server-time offset at login. Results are per-item — a rejected scan never fails the batch.

nodes.label: POST_SYNC_DUPLICATE (the honest limitation)
nodes.rationale: Two devices offline simultaneously can both admit the same guest QR. On sync the earlier scanned_at becomes ADMITTED and the later becomes DUPLICATE — but the second person is already inside. Inherent to admitting without a round trip, and the right trade: a gate that stalls is a worse failure than a rare double-admit. Mitigate, do not pretend to solve — never rewrite history to hide it (the DUPLICATE row stands), raise a POST_SYNC_DUPLICATE alert with both gate labels and timestamps, and prefetch known_codes per unit so offline devices catch same-ticket reuse locally where they can.

nodes.label: socket.io /live Namespace
nodes.rationale: Superuser JWT required on handshake, rooms per division. Events emitted ON COMMIT, never before: scan:admitted, scan:duplicate, scan:post_sync_duplicate, gate:offline. COALESCE at peak — emit aggregate counters on a 1s tick and stream only exceptions individually, because streaming every admission to every dashboard is how the socket layer becomes the bottleneck instead of the database. The dashboard is a CONSUMER, not a source of truth: it reconciles against a REST snapshot every 30s so a dropped socket cannot silently drift.

nodes.label: Ticket Reissue / Reprint
nodes.rationale: POST /api/admin/tickets/:id/reissue and POST /api/tickets/:id/reissue (agent reprinting their own, scoped by agent_id inside findTicketForAgent so another agent's ticket matches zero rows and 'not found' and 'not yours' are the same answer). Both share one reissueTicketCodes implementation rather than duplicating the rules that make a reprint safe. Same ticket id, request number, ticket number, buyer and tier, but NEW QR codes with the previous set REVOKED. The codes cannot be preserved because only sha256(payload) is stored; revoking them is what makes reprinting safe rather than a duplication hole, otherwise a 'lost' ticket that resurfaced would scan alongside the reprint. A REVOKED ticket cannot be reprinted at all.

nodes.label: Master Ticket Ledger and CSV Export
nodes.rationale: GET /api/admin/tickets + /filter-options. Ledger totals are a SQL aggregate over the whole filtered set, deliberately NOT a sum of returned rows — the row list is capped and would under-report. Both queries share one parameterised WHERE builder so the summary cards can never describe a different set than the table. /export shares the same builder but with its own fixed EXPORT_ROW_LIMIT (100,000, a backstop not a page size) instead of the client-suppliable limit, and returns text/csv with Content-Disposition. The frontend cannot reuse apiGet (it always calls res.json(), which throws on CSV), so apiClient.ts has a parallel apiDownload().

nodes.label: Premium Client Tracking (migration 015)
nodes.rationale: A record per premium guest with a running interaction timeline. Purchaser details already live on tickets; this holds what a ticket cannot — history over time BEFORE and around a sale — so records are created by hand and ticket_id is an optional link. Two tables, not a notes column, because the question is 'what did they say when, and who spoke to them', which needs rows with their own timestamps and authors or it degrades into one blob nobody can filter. Each interaction stores the author's NAME AT WRITE TIME, the same reasoning audit_logs uses for carrying no FK on actor_id: the log is read months later, possibly after that account is deactivated. Shared across all three superusers, not owned by one, because on event day a colleague must pick up a client whose usual contact is unreachable; PATCH is a genuine patch so two superusers editing different fields cannot clobber each other.

nodes.label: Client Pipeline Board (statuses as columns)
nodes.rationale: The five statuses (PROSPECT -> AWAITING_REPLY -> CONFIRMED -> TICKETED, plus DECLINED) ARE the kanban columns — no separate board-column concept was invented, so moving a card is exactly a status PATCH and the board stays a VIEW, not a parallel model that could disagree with the list. Movement is explicit ARROW CONTROLS, not drag-and-drop: HTML5 drag events do not fire on touch and this is used on phones as much as desktop, so a drag-only board would simply be broken there; the arrows also announce themselves to a screen reader, which draggable divs do not. They step one stage at a time; a jump straight from Prospect to Ticketed is done in the detail sheet where it is deliberate rather than a stray tap. Delete lives only in the detail sheet behind a two-step confirm naming the record and its update count, because deleting cascades the whole interaction timeline — the part that took months to accumulate.

nodes.label: clients.unit_id (migration 017)
nodes.rationale: A real FK, unlike units.sector's free text, because a unit is an existing row with an id so a client pointing at a nonexistent one is simply wrong. ON DELETE SET NULL, because retiring a unit must neither block nor destroy the record of conversations held while it existed. Nullable with NO BACKFILL — a premium guest is often a superuser's own contact rather than a unit's lead, so 'no unit' is a real permanent state, not missing data. The sector is NOT copied onto the row; it is one join away through units.sector and a second copy would drift.

nodes.label: Last Event Purchaser Import (migration 019)
nodes.rationale: clients gained referred_by, is_member and source; db:import-clients loads the 153 VIP/VVIP buyers from the previous event. No new tab — this IS the Clients screen's job and a second screen would split one pipeline in two. referred_by is deliberately FREE TEXT not an FK (unlike clients.unit_id): these are volunteers named on a WhatsApp list, most with no account and never will have one, so an FK would mean inventing one each or dropping the information. is_member is nullable on purpose: member, not a member, and not-yet-known are three distinct states. Names are transliterated from Kannada because the field is searched and typed on an English keyboard; source='LAST_EVENT_2025' marks them as imported so best-effort errors can be found and corrected. unit_id is left NULL because the source names SECTORS and a sector holds several units — guessing one would file a client under a unit head who never spoke to them.

nodes.label: Activities (migration 018)
nodes.rationale: The organiser's OWN task list, deliberately its own table rather than a generalisation of anything nearby: audit_logs records what the SYSTEM did automatically and is append-only evidence (nobody ticks off an audit row), and client_interactions is what was said to a specific premium guest whereas most tasks belong to no client at all. Merging them would give one table two owners, two lifecycles and two meanings for 'done'. done_at is a NULLABLE TIMESTAMP, not an is_done boolean: a boolean answers 'is it finished' but not 'when', and 'what did we close out last week' is a question this list gets asked — one column answers both and has no partner to drift out of sync with. The client sends done:true/false and the server stamps NOW(), because accepting a client-supplied timestamp would import whatever a shared phone's clock says. Totals on the cards are computed over the UNFILTERED set so '3 overdue' means the same thing whichever tab is selected.

nodes.label: Scan Log (/admin/scans)
nodes.rationale: GET /api/admin/scans records every scan ATTEMPT, not just admissions — a DUPLICATE burst at one gate is the signature of a copied ticket. All joins are LEFT so UNKNOWN_CODE rows, which have no ticket by definition, stay visible. Timestamps go out as UTC ISO and render in EVENT_TIME_ZONE (Asia/Riyadh), because a volunteer's phone is often still on their home timezone and the gate's clock is the one that matters.

nodes.label: db:provision-scanners (SCAN01-SCAN20)
nodes.rationale: Provisions 20 Gate Scanner rows into the existing gates table — a gate is a PLACE, not a person, so this is the same shared-PIN model every gate already uses, not a new account type. PINs are 6-digit numeric, deliberately not alphanumeric, because GateLoginSchema validates digits-only and the scanner login page's numeric keypad strips anything else as it's typed. Idempotent but REISSUES all 20 PINs on every run, so it is a provisioning tool, not a rotation tool.

nodes.label: db:provision-superusers (ADMIN01-ADMIN03)
nodes.rationale: Provisions the 3 real Super User accounts, distinct from db:seed's disposable admin1/admin2/admin3 sharing one hardcoded password. 8-character passwords via lib/passwordGen.ts's generateSecurePassword(), the same unambiguous alphabet and guaranteed upper/lower/digit mix bulk-rotate uses. email is left NULL; nothing fabricates an address nobody supplied. It deactivates everything that is not ADMIN01-ADMIN03 because SuperAdmin@2026 is committed to this repository and was reachable on a live deployment. Note the loop: db:seed's upsert sets is_active=TRUE so re-running it re-enables them, which is why the seed is the only script with a NODE_ENV guard.

nodes.label: db:provision-demo-agent (DEMO01)
nodes.rationale: A TEMPORARY unit + agent for recording a demo video, with --destroy to remove them. Its own unit and its own sector='DEMO' on purpose: tickets filmed on camera are real rows, so a demo on a real unit would land in that unit's ledger and its sector's analytics as genuine sales and have to be unpicked by hand. --destroy DELETES rather than revokes — a demo ticket was never a sale that got cancelled, and REVOKED rows would footnote revenue totals forever — in FK order (scan_logs -> tickets -> sessions -> agents -> unit) since every one of those FKs is ON DELETE RESTRICT. The audit_logs rows for both halves are deliberately kept. Run --destroy once filming is done; the invite PIN is published to anyone who watches the recording.

nodes.label: Back Navigation (useDismissOnBack)
nodes.rationale: Overlays are React state, not routes, so Android's hardware Back used to leave the page and lose whatever the agent was doing. lib/useDismissOnBack.ts pushes one history entry when an overlay opens and closes the overlay on popstate; closing by button pops that entry back off so the stack cannot accumulate dead entries. AdminShell also renders a back-to-overview control on every section except /dashboard — the nav rail moves sideways but offered no way up, and on a phone it scrolls out of view.

nodes.label: Two-Layer Route Protection
nodes.rationale: NEITHER LAYER PROTECTS DATA. middleware.ts decodes the cookie payload WITHOUT verifying the signature — the signing secret lives on the API, not the web tier — so it is navigation UX only and a forged cookie reaches an empty shell. ProtectedRoute waits for GET /api/auth/session, which the API validated properly, and covers client-side navigations. The real boundary is requireAgent/requireSuperuser on every endpoint; do not add a frontend check and consider a route secured. Sharing JWT_SECRET with Next to verify in middleware was REJECTED: it would let the web tier mint tokens, a worse trade than an empty shell. Route groups produce no URL segment, so adding a page means adding it to ROUTE_ROLES AND matcher.

nodes.label: Two Login Surfaces (/login vs /management)
nodes.rationale: /login is event staff (Unit Gateway, Agent Login, First-Time Setup) and carries NO administrative entry points at all: several hundred agents use it and none should be looking at a door they must never open. /management holds Super User and Unit Admin sign-in plus a link to the gate scanner. THE PATH IS SEGREGATION, NOT SECRECY — a URL is not a credential; /management is in the repo, the bundle and browser history, and what protects those roles is unchanged (passwords, requireSuperuser/requireUnitAdmin/requireScanAccess, the rate limiter). Named /management and not /admin precisely because ROUTE_ROLES guards the whole /admin prefix with SUPERUSER, so a login form there would redirect its own users away before they could sign in. Both are in PUBLIC_ROUTES; /management is listed rather than merely omitted from matcher so a signed-in visitor is bounced home instead of shown a role chooser. Gate Scanner is a link to the existing public /scanner/login, not a fourth inline form.

nodes.label: Postmortem — Every Gate Scan Failed
nodes.rationale: insertScanLog used ON CONFLICT (client_scan_id) DO NOTHING, but migration 001 creates that arbiter as a PARTIAL unique index (WHERE client_scan_id IS NOT NULL, because online scans that never queued carry NULL). Postgres can only infer a partial index as an arbiter when the conflict target repeats its predicate; a bare target matches no usable index and raises 42P10. That aborted the transaction in resolveScan(), rolling back admitGuestCode()'s UPDATE with it — so the QR never flipped to SCANNED, no scan_logs row was written, and /api/scan/verify 500'd on EVERY scan. The scanner then did exactly what the spec tells it to do with a 5xx: queue and show a green 'Admitted — pending sync'. So the gate LOOKED like it was working while nothing reached the database. Two fixes: the conflict target now carries the predicate, and a 5xx is no longer reported as bad wifi (ScanFailureKind gives a red Server error badge, distinct from amber Offline).

nodes.label: Known Debt Register
nodes.rationale: 1) npm audit flags nodemailer and sharp/postcss transitively via Next, none on a request path. 2) No true perforation notches — background-coloured cutout circles break in print and email. 3) Socket rooms are a single superusers room; no gate:offline heartbeat, so 'active gate' is inferred from recent scan activity. 4) The sequences are in use again via migration 016; the entry is kept so the earlier 'drop these' note is not acted on by mistake. 5) The seed creates no tickets. 6) Premium LOCATION rows are issued but never printed, inert not harmful. 7) units.sector is free text with no FK or CHECK, so a hand-written UPDATE could create a phantom sector — the filter list derives from DISTINCT sector so a typo shows as an extra dropdown entry rather than silently swallowing rows. 8) units.agent_invite_pin is a readable COPY whose verification path is the bcrypt hash; a manual UPDATE to one alone drifts them and the failure mode is a unit head reciting a PIN that does not work.

nodes.label: Not Yet Built
nodes.rationale: Divisions/units/agents CRUD; ticket revocation FROM THE UI (the reissue path revokes codes, not tickets); real QR encoding; gate:offline heartbeat; a superuser UI for editing zone coverage (direct SQL only); replacing the placeholder 10/10/10 zone split with the real geographic assignment; a way for a unit admin to ROTATE their own agent_invite_pin (they can now view it via GET /api/unit-admin/invite-pin, but changing it is db:provision-units or direct SQL — and remember to write both columns).

nodes.label: build:shared Compiled-Output Gotcha
nodes.rationale: @pravasi/shared is consumed as COMPILED output, not source. Any edit under packages/shared/src is invisible to both tiers until npm run build:shared is re-run. This is the #1 cause of 'I changed the constant but nothing happened.'

nodes.label: No Lint, No Automated Tests
nodes.rationale: No ESLint config exists in any workspace and no automated test suite exists — TESTING.md is a manual E2E checklist and is, today, the entire test suite. Before calling any change to auth, ticketing or scanning done, walk the relevant TESTING.md section by hand. typecheck is the only automated correctness gate and must be run on both backend and frontend.
